title: Where exactly is the line between AI-assisted and AI-generated art?
author: Felizzle
selftext:
I understand why these rules requiring developers to disclose AI usage exist. It's largely thanks to the very vocal community of passionate and completely rational AI-haters who seem to believe *"human = good :), AI = evil :("*. I accept that these rules exist, even though I find them beyond ridiculous. But where exactly do we draw the line?

A few hypothetical examples:

* I generate an image using AI, then redraw it myself in Paint, pixel by pixel, like every respectable human artist should. Still AI art?
* I pay a professional artist to create assets for me. How can I possibly know whether they used AI somewhere in their workflow?
* I create artwork myself but use Photoshop's AI-powered background removal. Is that AI art?
* I generate an AI image, open Photoshop, increase brightness by 1, decrease contrast by 0.5, and increase saturation by 0.3. My own creation now, right?

I know some of these examples sound ridiculous, but that's precisely my point. They are ridiculous because the rule itself is ridiculous. **Where does AI-assisted end and AI-generated begin? Who decides, and how is any of this supposed to be enforced consistently?**

To me, this is the same as requiring developers to disclose whether they used VSCode or any other IDE instead of Notepad, because apparently using more powerful tools makes your work less legitimate. AI is everywhere nowadays, it's integrated into Photoshop, coding environments, and countless other tools. Not using AI at this point often just means deliberately slowing yourself down.

I'd genuinely appreciate input from anyone familiar with Steamworks policies or the legal side of this.

**Are there actually clear, enforceable definitions or thresholds for AI-generated content?** What about legitimate workflows that involve AI somewhere in the process but produce manually created assets?

**Are there legitimate ways to avoid triggering these disclosure requirements, or is virtually any involvement of AI enough?**

I'm not looking for ways to deceive Steam. I just find the whole distinction increasingly arbitrary and would love to understand where the actual boundaries are.

comments.author: PhantomZenithOrigin
comments.body:
There is no line defined.

I interpret Steam's guidelines as "Is there anything in the game that players will see that you pressed \[Generate\] and then simply used it as an asset without touching it?"

replies.author: Felizzle
replies.body: I understand your interpretation, but wouldn't that mean the "+1 brightness, -1 contrast" example technically wouldn't require disclosure either, since I *modified* the AI-generated image? That's exactly where I think the distinction becomes problematic, like how much modification is enough? Anyways, thanks for the input and good luck getting rid of your Suno garbage!

replies.author: PhantomZenithOrigin
replies.body:
Yes, however that's not the intent.

The true measure of 'where the line is', is that if it feels like you didn't do truly 'transform' it, then you need to disclose it.

What many don't get is that by over-defining the rules it permits people to game the system, but if you leave things underdefined then you're able to make rulings individually and as you see fit, which is how any company would want things to be.

**The truth of the matter is that as a creator, YOU know where the line is.**  You know it in your heart where that line is, and nobody is going to set out the clear cut rules for you to skirt around.

replies.author: Limp_Bus3865
replies.body: and if you used AI for assiting you with coding, you should disclose that as well

replies.author: PhantomZenithOrigin
replies.body: Steam specifically doesn't require that to be disclosed, they are quite clear about that on your Steamworks publisher dashboard.

comments.author: lyeeedar
comments.body:
The distinction IS totally arbitrary, and nonsense. But the disclosure at the moment is fine. Put it on, the people who will.have a tantrum about ai will avoid the game (a small group, all in all) and you can go about your day without harassment. Simply the ai disclosure box existing on your game will be enough to make them avoid, regardless of what's written in it.

It becomes an issue if you try to hide it. Its really really REALLY not worth the effort. Will you get a fraction more sales? Maybe. Will you put yourself at risk of being review bombed by customers who feel 'tricked'? Far more likely. Better to cull them early than allow them to kill the game by high return rates and negative reviews.

Personally I just put something vague like "used in the production" and call it a day. The people who cared about that were never customers anyway.

replies.author: Felizzle
replies.body: Thanks for the advice, that actually sounds like the most sensible approach for as long as these rules remain in place.

comments.author: itix
comments.body: The problem with AI generated 2D image art is that once you have a few, you have seen them all. They are samey with noticeable patterns and imperfections. It is like a voluntary "AI used here" badge that screams over everything.

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
Don't worry about the disclosure.   
Even the AAA studios are using AI tools.   
It will very soon just become accepted as the standard. 

The difference is really the degree of human input, quality control and input. 

Did you fix those slop errors or not?   
Did you manage some semblance of good art direction so your style looks homogeneous and posh or not?  

Did you give your game a unique aesthetic or does it look like basic generic text-2-imgage Ai generations? 

Does the game look and play like there was a lot of human thought put in to it or does it look like you one prompted a generic clone of something everyone is already familiar with? 

Did you show the players something unique and interesting or not?

comments.author: hyperg8_games
comments.body: the brightness +1 trick made me laugh, but players dont read the label anyway, they spot raw unpolished output instantly and some yell slop even at human-made art. I use AI a lot myself, polish is what counts imho

comments.author: KS-Wolf-1978
comments.body: -Load a LoRA trained on your art.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
It doesn't matter what you do, you'll be scrutinized  for it, good or bad. I say just make an effort to stand out with quality.

Theres a game on NES called Little Nemo, and sometimes when you get struck while inside a frog mouth, half your body will appear on the far end of the screen a little bit. Is it a bad game? Yes, but this detail makes you notice it more.

comments.author: JDad67
comments.body: If a non artist creates something pretty it’s ai-generated. If an artist does it (even with the exact same steps and outcome) it’s, at worst, AI assisted.
